new_statements.translation: In Quichua the accent generally falls on the penultimate syllable. The few exceptions to this rule are set out in the grammatical sketch. [p.155] ... When the form -i is used, the accent must be written on the final vowel of the noun: B., T. yacúi, L. yacupi 'in the river'. [p.158] ... -ngahua (B.), -ngapa (L.), -ngáj (T.) express purpose ... note that T. -ngáj carries the accent. [p.160] ... -ga marks emphasis ... usually the accent stays on the penultimate syllable of the word to which -ga is added: yáyaga 'what about your father?' [p.162]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable. The only exceptions are morphological, and in the L. (Napo/Loreto = qvo) dialect most of them do not arise: the locative is -pi (yacupi, penult) rather than the stress-attracting -i of Bobonaza and Tena, and the purposive is -ngapa rather than Tena's final-stressed -ngáj; the emphatic enclitic -ga is extrametrical (stress stays on the host's penult). Orr 1978 (pp.7-10) confirms this for the Napo dialect: the final-syllable stress of Pastaza/Tena locative -i and progressive -u-, of Tena 3sg present verbs (pichán, shamún, micún) and desiderative -nai-, is absent in Napo, which keeps -pi, -ju-, -nayan. Orr & Levinsohn 1991 (p.9 n.) add that the interrogative enclitic -ta does not move stress, giving antepenult stress in words of 3+ syllables, while accusative -ta yields regular penult stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in Orr & Wrisley 1981, Orr 1978 or Orr & Levinsohn 1991. (O'Rourke & Swanson 2013 report optional initial secondary stress for the sister Tena variety; Orr 1962/1975, Pastaza base, says stress is accompanied by high pitch and that terminal juncture carries a phrase stress.)
new_statements.exceptions: Written accent only where stress is not penultimate: stress-attracting suffixes -i (locative; B., T. only, L. uses -pi), -ngáj (T. only), and, per Orr 1978, Tena-only final stress in 3sg present verbs and desiderative -nai-; enclitic -ga (and, per Orr & Levinsohn 1991, interrogative -ta) do not shift stress, yielding antepenultimate stress (yáyaga; esdrújula forms with -ta). Orr 1962/1975 (Pastaza base) calls stress 'nonpredictable and therefore phonemic' because of these final-stressed word classes (wasíy, cagráy, rimáun, mikúun, siriún).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('cae en la penúltima sílaba' of the word; enclitics -ga/-ta treated as outside the stress domain). Practical-orthography statement in a dictionary appendix, based on SIL fieldwork in the three Oriente dialects; not instrumental.
new_statements.identity_note: The deciding statement (Orr & Wrisley 1981) is written for the three Ecuadorian Oriente dialects jointly: B = Puyo/Bobonaza (Northern Pastaza Quichua, nort2973/qvz), T = Tena/Arajuno/Ahuano (Tena Lowland Quichua, tena1240/quw), and L = Loreto/Payamino and the Napo from the Suno to Nuevo Rocafuerte, which is the Ecuadorian part of napo1242/qvo (SIL codes the dictionary quw+qvo+qvz; Orr 1978 calls this L dialect 'Napo' and extends it to the Putumayo and lower Aguarico). The penult rule holds for all three; the L-specific facts (no stress-attracting -i or -ngáj, invariant penult stress) come from the L forms in the same appendix and from Orr 1978 pp.7-10 and Orr & Levinsohn 1991 p.9 n. (the latter explicitly for the Napo river in NE Ecuador and northern Peru and the Putumayo). Caution: Orr 1962/1975 'Ecuador Quichua phonology', which SIL, Glottolog and our earlier survey attach to napo1242, describes the Puyo Pongo dialect (Pastaza, nort2973) with dialect notes for Dos Ríos (Tena area, quw); its 'nonpredictable/phonemic, most frequently penultimate' statement should not be catalogued as qvo. Zariquiey 2004 and Moffitt 2019, the two modern descriptions of the Peruvian Napo (qvo proper), are silent on stress. Nuckolls & Swanson 2018/2020 explicitly exclude the below-Coca (qvo) dialect.

sources.note: p.155: accent 'por lo general' on the penultimate syllable; few exceptions given in the grammar notes: locative -i in B. and T. dialects takes written accent on the final vowel (yacúi) but the L. (Napo/Loreto = qvo) dialect uses -pi (yacupi) with no shift (p.158); purposive -ngáj of T. carries the accent, vs L. -ngapa (p.160); enclitic -ga leaves the accent on the penult of its host, yáyaga (p.162). Dialect key p.iii: B = Puyo/Bobonaza, T = Tena/Arajuno/Ahuano, L = Payamino from Loreto down and the Napo from the Suno to Nuevo Rocafuerte.
